0.title: Glorifying God Together
0.essay:
Worship is what we were made for. The first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism asks, “What is the chief end of man?” and answers, “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.” Every human being worships something. The question is never whether we will worship, but what, and how.

A debated subject

Yet worship has become one of the most debated subjects in the church. Some think of it mainly as music. Others argue about styles, instruments, lighting and length. Some treat Sunday as a day like any other; others as a day of strict rules. Behind these practical questions lie deeper ones. What is worship? Who decides how God should be worshipped? What should happen when the church gathers? And what is the Lord’s Day for?

God seeks worshippers

Jesus said, “the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him” (John 4:23). God is not only worthy of worship; he seeks worshippers. That is an invitation.

The chapters

What Is Worship?; Worshipping God His Way; What Happens When the Church Gathers; Singing to the Lord; The Lord’s Day; and Worship with All of Life. Two questions are handled with the main views and a verdict: how Scripture governs worship, and how the Sabbath applies to Christians.

1.title: What Is Worship?
1.essay:
Worship is giving God the honour he deserves. The English word comes from “worth-ship”: to worship God is to declare and treat him as supremely worthy. In Scripture it includes bowing down, serving, praising, thanking and offering. It is an attitude of the heart and acts of the body and voice.

A response

We do not worship to get God’s attention. We worship because he has revealed himself and acted. “Oh come, let us worship and bow down; let us kneel before the LORD, our Maker! For he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture” (Psalm 95:6–7). Psalm 95 has been used as a call to worship for centuries. It begins with joyful noise and thanksgiving, grounded in God’s greatness as Creator, and moves to bowing and kneeling, grounded in his covenant care. Then it warns, “do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 95:8). Worship begins with who God is and what he has done, and it must reach the heart. That is why worship and Scripture belong together.

In spirit and truth

The Samaritan woman raised a question about the right place to worship. Jesus moved the conversation from place to person: not this mountain or Jerusalem, but “in spirit and truth” (John 4:23–24). Worship must be in spirit: from the heart, by the Holy Spirit, not mere outward form. And it must be in truth: according to God’s revealed truth, and centred on Christ, who is the truth. Hearts without truth produce sincere idolatry. Truth without hearts produces dead orthodoxy. God wants both.

And notice that the Father is seeking such worshippers. Worship is not our attempt to find God. It is our response to the God who has found us.

Through Christ

We cannot approach a holy God on our own. Christ is our great high priest, and through him we have access to the Father. “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15). Animal sacrifices have ended in Christ, but Christian worship still has sacrifices. One is praise. The other follows at once: “Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God” (Hebrews 13:16). Praise without kindness is empty.

Reverence and joy

Believers have received a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and the right response is gratitude: “let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews 12:28–29). The God of grace is still the God of Sinai. “Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling” (Psalm 2:11). Worship that is only joyful becomes shallow; worship that is only solemn becomes cold.

When Isaiah saw the Lord high and lifted up, he heard the seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), and he cried out, “Woe is me! For I am lost” (Isaiah 6:5). After his lips were cleansed, he answered God’s call: “Here I am! Send me” (Isaiah 6:8). True worship moves from seeing God, to confession, to forgiveness, to obedience.

Idols and audiences

The opposite of true worship is not no worship but idolatry. Human hearts are idol factories. We worship money, comfort, approval, success or family whenever we look to them for what only God can give. True worship dethrones these idols.

In gathered worship God is the audience, and the whole congregation are participants. Leaders and musicians are not performers for a crowd but servants helping the people worship together.

A man has always judged Sunday services by whether he “got something out of it”. Studying worship, he realises he has made himself the audience. He begins coming to church with a different question: “How can I give God the praise he deserves, and help others to do the same?” Strangely, he now gets far more out of it.

All of life, and gathered

Paul says that presenting our bodies as living sacrifices is our “spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1), so all of life can be worship. But Scripture also calls God’s people to gather. These are not rivals. The gathered worship of Sunday shapes the scattered worship of Monday, and a whole week of obedience flows back into Sunday praise.

Before church next Sunday, ask yourself: am I going mainly to receive something, or mainly to give God glory?

For reflection

How would you now define worship in your own words? Why must it be both “in spirit” and “in truth”? What idols compete with God for your worship? How could you prepare your heart for gathered worship this Sunday?

2.title: Worshipping God His Way
2.essay:
Can we worship God however we like, as long as we are sincere? Scripture says no. God cares not only that he is worshipped, but how.

Unauthorised fire

At the very start of Israel’s priesthood, Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, “offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them”. Fire came out from the LORD and consumed them. Moses explained: “Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.” And Aaron “held his peace” (Leviticus 10:1–3). These men had seen God’s glory on Sinai (Exodus 24:9–11). They were priests, at the right place, offering to the right God. But they did it in a way he had not commanded. Aaron did not argue, because God’s word was clear: he is holy and must be approached on his terms.

Neither add nor take away

The second commandment forbids making images to worship God, even images meant to honour him (Exodus 20:4–6). The golden calf was presented as the LORD who brought Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 32:4–5), yet it was idolatry. As Israel entered Canaan, they would be tempted to worship the LORD the way the nations worshipped their gods. Moses forbade it: “Everything that I command you, you shall be careful to do. You shall not add to it or take from it” (Deuteronomy 12:32). Worship is to be shaped by God’s word, not by the surrounding culture.

Jesus quoted Isaiah against religious leaders whose traditions had overridden God’s commands: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men” (Matthew 15:8–9). Sincere-looking worship can still be empty.

Even a king could not invent his own approach to God. Uzziah was strong and successful, but when he grew proud he entered the temple to burn incense, a task God had given only to the priests, and he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

We receive worship

The principle is clear: God decides how he is to be approached. We do not invent worship; we receive it. That is a protection as well as a restriction. It frees churches from the endless pressure to innovate, and it frees worshippers from having their consciences bound by human inventions.

So what has God commanded for gathered worship? The New Testament shows the essential elements: the reading of Scripture (1 Timothy 4:13), preaching (2 Timothy 4:2), prayer (1 Timothy 2:1), singing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (Colossians 3:16), baptism and the Lord’s Supper (Matthew 28:19; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26), giving (1 Corinthians 16:2) and the confession of faith. These are the heart of Christian worship in every culture and age.

Order and peace

The Corinthian gatherings were chaotic, and Paul gave instructions: everything for building up, speakers in turn, silence when needed. The reason is theological: “For God is not a God of confusion but of peace” (1 Corinthians 14:33). Orderly worship reflects the character of God. Freedom in worship is never freedom from order: “all things should be done decently and in order” (1 Corinthians 14:40).

How does Scripture govern worship?

The normative principle, held by Lutherans, Anglicans and many evangelicals, says that anything not forbidden in Scripture may be included in worship. The regulative principle, held by the Reformed tradition, says that only what Scripture commands or warrants may be included as an element of worship.

The regulative principle fits Leviticus 10, Deuteronomy 12:32 and Jesus’ rebuke in Matthew 15 best. But it must be applied with wisdom. It governs the elements of worship — what we do. It does not dictate the circumstances — when, where, how long, which building, which tune — which are ordered by wisdom and decency. Drama, liturgical dance and religious images are additions; a sound system and a printed order of service are circumstances.

Some who hold the regulative principle exclude musical instruments, seeing them as part of the temple worship that ended with Christ. But the Psalms, which the church is told to sing, repeatedly call for instruments (Psalm 150), and they are heard in heaven, where the elders each hold a harp (Revelation 5:8). Instruments that serve congregational singing are a legitimate help, as long as they support the singing rather than replace or drown it.

Plain, and full

A church’s leaders feel under pressure to make the service more exciting with drama, video clips and a short message. They study Scripture together and decide instead to give more time to Bible reading, congregational prayer and singing. Some visitors find it plain at first. But over time members say they have never felt closer to God in worship.

When you evaluate worship, do you ask first, “Was it moving?” or “Was it what God has asked for?”

For reflection

Why do you think God cares how he is worshipped, not only that he is worshipped? What is the difference between an element and a circumstance? Is there anything in your church’s worship that comes more from tradition or culture than from Scripture? How does the regulative principle protect worshippers’ consciences?

3.title: What Happens When the Church Gathers
3.essay:
Gathered worship is a meeting between God and his people. In it God speaks to us and we respond to him. Seeing worship as a dialogue helps us understand each part of it.

God calls, and we confess

Worship begins with God’s invitation, often a call to worship from Scripture. We do not come on our own initiative but because he summons us. Then, coming before a holy God, we acknowledge our sin and hear his assurance of forgiveness in Christ (1 John 1:9). That keeps worship humble and centred on grace.

God speaks through his word

The public reading of Scripture and the preaching of the word are the centre of Christian worship. After the exile, the whole people gathered and asked Ezra to bring the Book of the Law. They stood as it was opened, worshipped and listened from early morning until midday. Levites helped them understand: “They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). The people wept, then celebrated, because they had understood. This is the root of expository preaching: God’s word read, and explained.

Paul gave Timothy three public tasks: “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, to teaching” (1 Timothy 4:13). Then he urged, “Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching. Persist in this, for by so doing you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16). It is a matter of life and death.

His last charge was more solemn still, given in the presence of God and Christ the Judge: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching” (2 Timothy 4:2). The reason was that people would want teachers who told them what they wanted to hear (2 Timothy 4:3). A preacher’s job is not to be popular but faithful. Preaching is not a lecture or a pep talk. It is God speaking through a messenger, explaining his word and applying it to his people. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). A church that pushes preaching to the edges has misplaced the centre.

We pray

The first thing Paul urges for the gathered church is prayer of every kind, for all people, including rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2). The aim is a peaceful life and the salvation of the lost, because God “desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2:4). Congregational prayer has a missionary heart, and it is one of the most neglected parts of worship today.

We sing and give

Through song, believers praise God and teach one another (Colossians 3:16). And giving is an act of worship too: an offering of thanks to God and a sharing with those in need (2 Corinthians 9:12–13).

God seals and blesses

In baptism and the Lord’s Supper God confirms his promises to believers in visible signs. And worship often ends with a benediction, God’s blessing spoken over his people as they go out: “The LORD bless you and keep you” (Numbers 6:24).

The shape may vary from church to church. But the elements are the same, and the movement from God’s word to our response is constant.

Everyone takes part

In New Testament worship the congregation is not passive. Everyone sings, prays — at least by saying “Amen” — and listens actively. Paul expects even an outsider to be able to say “Amen” to what is said (1 Corinthians 14:16).

Worship is for believers, but outsiders may come in, and Paul wanted them to understand and be convicted, “and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you” (1 Corinthians 14:25). Clarity serves the gospel.

From late arrival to high point

A Christian used to arrive late and leave straight after the sermon. Learning that worship is a dialogue with God, he begins to come early, pray for the service, listen to the Scripture reading as God’s voice, and stay for the benediction. Worship becomes the high point of his week.

During the sermon, are you listening for information, or for God’s word to you?

For reflection

How does seeing worship as a dialogue between God and his people change your view of the service? Why is preaching central? How could your church give more attention to congregational prayer? Which part of gathered worship do you find hardest to engage with, and why?

4.title: Singing to the Lord
4.essay:
The Bible is full of singing. Moses and Miriam sang after the Red Sea. David wrote psalms. Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn after the Last Supper (Matthew 26:30). Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight. And the book of Revelation rings with songs before the throne. God’s people are a singing people.

Why we sing

Singing joins truth and emotion. It engages the mind, the heart and the body. It helps us remember what we believe. And it unites a congregation, so that many voices become one praise.

An elderly woman with dementia no longer recognises her family. But when her pastor visits and begins a hymn she has known since childhood, she sings every verse with him. The truths she sang for decades are stored deeper than her memory can reach.

Upward and outward

“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God” (Colossians 3:16). Singing is one way the word of Christ lives richly in a church. It is directed to God, and it teaches one another. Then Paul widens the circle: “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Colossians 3:17). Sunday singing and weekday living are both worship.

In Ephesians, being filled with the Spirit shows itself in “addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart” (Ephesians 5:19). A Spirit-filled church is a singing church.

Because singing teaches, the words matter. A song that is musically beautiful but theologically empty does not teach well. Look at the words of the songs you sang last Sunday: what did they teach you about God?

What makes a good song

A good song for worship is true to Scripture. It focuses on God and his works, not mainly on our feelings. It is singable by a congregation, not only by a soloist. It has enough depth to bear repetition and to carry people through suffering. And it is sung from the heart.

The Psalms

The Psalms are God’s own songbook, inspired by the Spirit. They cover every human emotion: praise, thanksgiving, confession, lament, anger, trust and hope. Churches that never sing psalms lose the language of lament and the honesty of the psalmists. A church that rediscovers them will find its prayers and songs deepened.

And singing is missionary. “Oh sing to the LORD a new song; sing to the LORD, all the earth! … Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!” (Psalm 96:1–3). When the church sings God’s praise, it proclaims his greatness to the world. In a Philippian jail, beaten and in stocks, “Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them” (Acts 16:25). Their singing in suffering was itself a witness.

Only psalms?

Some Reformed churches sing only the biblical Psalms in worship, reasoning that only inspired songs should be sung. Most churches sing psalms alongside hymns and songs written by believers.

Paul’s phrase “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” most naturally refers to a variety of songs, and the New Testament itself contains Christ-centred hymns (Philippians 2:6–11; Colossians 1:15–20; Revelation 5:9–10). The church may sing faithful songs that celebrate Christ by name. But exclusive psalmody reminds us of something important: the Psalms deserve a large place in our singing.

Scripture does not prescribe a musical style. Churches should choose music that serves congregational singing and fits the words, and members should bear with one another’s preferences in love.

The song of heaven

In Revelation the redeemed sing a new song to the Lamb: “Worthy are you to take the scroll and to open its seals, for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9). Then the circle widens to myriads of angels. The song of heaven is about Christ and his cross. If that is the song of eternity, it should be the centre of our songs now. Our singing here is rehearsal for that day.

For reflection

Why do you think God wants his people to sing, not only to speak? Choose a favourite hymn or song: what does it teach about God? How could you make more use of the Psalms in your singing and praying? Read Revelation 5:9–14. How should the song of heaven shape our singing now?

5.title: The Lord’s Day
5.essay:
From the beginning, God built a rhythm into creation. He worked six days and rested on the seventh: “So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy” (Genesis 2:3).

The Sabbath

In the Ten Commandments God told Israel, “Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exodus 20:8), resting from work as he had rested. The rest reached everyone in the household — servants, foreigners, even animals. It was a day to remember that the world belongs to God. In Deuteronomy the Sabbath also recalled the rescue from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15): slaves get no rest, but God’s freed people do.

Lord of the Sabbath

When the Pharisees accused Jesus’ disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking grain, he answered with David’s example and then with two great claims: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27–28). The Sabbath was made for our good, not as a burden. And the one who made it has authority to interpret it — and to fulfil it. He healed on the Sabbath and rejected the Pharisees’ burdensome rules. And he offered what the Sabbath only pictured: “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28).

The shadow and the substance

False teachers in Colossae were judging believers for not keeping food laws and holy days. Paul answered, “Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16–17). A shadow is real, but it points to something greater. Now that the substance has come, believers should not be judged by the shadow.

Hebrews argues that God’s rest was not finally given in Joshua’s day: “So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). It is entered by ceasing from our own works and trusting Christ, and it will be completed in glory. Every Lord’s Day is a foretaste of that eternal rest.

The Lord’s Day

The early church gathered on the first day of the week, the day of the resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). John calls it “the Lord’s day” (Revelation 1:10). It is not the Jewish Sabbath moved to Sunday with all its regulations. It is the day of new creation, when the risen Christ meets his people.

At Troas the church gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, and Paul talked with them until midnight. A young man fell asleep, fell from a window and was taken up dead, and Paul restored him to life (Acts 20:7–12). The gathering was so precious that it lasted all night.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath?

Many Reformed Christians hold that the fourth commandment is a moral law for all time, so that Sunday is “the Christian Sabbath”, to be kept holy by rest from ordinary work and recreation. Others hold that the Sabbath belonged to the Mosaic covenant — “a sign between me and you” (Exodus 31:13) — and is fulfilled in Christ, so that Christians are not bound by a weekly Sabbath law, though they gather on the Lord’s Day.

The Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ. Colossians 2:16–17 calls it a shadow, and Romans 14 lets believers differ over days: “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (Romans 14:5). Of the Ten Commandments, the Sabbath alone is not repeated as a command in the New Testament. Yet gathering on the Lord’s Day is the clear apostolic pattern and must not be neglected (Hebrews 10:25), and the rhythm of rest God built into creation remains wise.

Christians who keep Sunday as a Sabbath and those who do not should not judge one another (Romans 14:4–6). Both should honour the Lord’s Day with gathered worship.

Rest as a gift

The principle of rest remains good. Human beings are not machines. A regular rhythm of rest is a gift from our Creator and an act of trust: we stop working because God, not we, holds the world together. Sunday, set apart for worship, fellowship and rest, is a blessing to be enjoyed rather than a law to be feared.

A family has filled Sundays with sport, errands and work emails, squeezing in church when they can. They decide to treat Sunday as a gift: church in the morning, a long family lunch, a walk, time with friends, no work email. They do not make it a list of rules. But their whole week is steadier because it now begins with worship and rest.

Does your Sunday look different from your other days? Does it point you to Christ, your true rest?

For reflection

What does the Sabbath in creation teach us about God and about ourselves? How does Jesus fulfil the Sabbath? How can Christians with different views of the Sabbath avoid judging one another? What would it look like for you to receive the Lord’s Day as a gift this week?

6.title: Worship with All of Life
6.essay:
Gathered worship matters, but it is not the whole of worship. “I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship” (Romans 12:1).

A whole life reshaped

Paul begins the practical part of Romans with worship. The motive is the mercies of God described in the first eleven chapters. The offering is our bodies, our whole selves. And the means is transformation: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Worship is a whole life reshaped by grace.

Worship God rejects

The prophets warned that worship without obedience offends God. Through Amos he spoke with shocking bluntness: “I hate, I despise your feasts, and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies” (Amos 5:21). He rejected their offerings and would not listen to their songs, because the worshippers were trampling the poor. What he wanted instead was this: “But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24). Isaiah and Micah said the same. God does not want religion instead of righteousness. Songs on Sunday mean little if our lives deny them on Monday.

True worship and holy living cannot be separated. The same Spirit who leads us to praise God leads us to love our neighbour. Worship that does not change how we live is not true worship.

Worship in ordinary life

“So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Paul wrote that after a long discussion of food offered to idols. Even something as ordinary as eating and drinking can glorify God, and the principle covers “whatever you do”. Work, family life, rest, hospitality, friendship and service can all be done to God’s glory. The farmer, the nurse, the parent and the student can offer their days as worship.

Daniel, a senior official in Babylon, kept praying three times a day toward Jerusalem even when it became a crime punishable by death (Daniel 6:10). His daily work in a pagan government and his worship of God were not separate, and faithfulness in both gave him courage when he was tested.

A nurse working night shifts often misses Sunday services and feels her faith is weak. Her pastor reminds her that caring for the sick, done for Christ, is worship, and helps her find a midweek Bible study and a way to be at church at least twice a month. She begins to see her work as an offering.

The gathered church still matters

All of life can be worship, but not everything is equally so. The gathered worship of the church has a special place: it is where God has promised to meet his people through word and sacrament. The truth that all of life is worship should never become a reason to neglect the gathered church.

Worship in suffering

Job, having lost everything, “fell on the ground and worshiped. And he said, ‘Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD’” (Job 1:20–21). Worship in suffering may be the purest worship of all, because it honours God for who he is, not for what he gives.

Worship and mission

Mission exists because worship does not. The goal of evangelism is to bring more worshippers to God from every nation, “in order that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15:9). When the church worships, it shows the world what it was made for.

Worship for ever

Worship is not a temporary activity. It is the eternal occupation of the redeemed. The Bible ends where it began, in a garden with the tree of life, though now it is a city too. The curse is gone, and “the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his servants will worship him. They will see his face” (Revelation 22:3–4). All of history moves toward this. Everything in our worship now, gathered and scattered, is preparation for that day.

If someone watched your life this week, would they see a worshipper of God?

For reflection

What does it mean to present your body as a living sacrifice? Read Amos 5:21–24: what might God say about the gap between our Sunday worship and our weekday lives? How can your work, family life or rest be offered to God this week? How does the promise of Revelation 22:3–4 shape your worship now?
